meta.name: Sourdough Pizza Dough
meta.description: Sourdough variant of the NY-Style Pizza Dough. Replaces commercial yeast with 100g active starter, uses fermentolyse + stretch-and-fold instead of autolyse + stand mixer, and adds diastatic malt powder to compensate for acid-inhibited Maillard browning at 550°F.

change_log.summary: Add scaling research block with 1–2× tested range, ingredient behavior classification, and process caveats for bulk fermentation timing and vessel size.
Add sugar substitute instruction to fermentolyse step — 5g granulated sugar in place of diastatic malt when unavailable.
Initial recipe from multi-agent research synthesis. Sourdough variant of NY-Style Pizza Dough v1.4.0 — fermentolyse, stretch-and-fold, diastatic malt, no olive oil.

ingredients.name: Bread Flour
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 5/5 pure SD recipes use flour; 3/5 specify bread flour
ingredients.rationale: Bread flour (13%+ protein) browns reliably at 550°F and develops strong gluten for stretch

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.rationale: Maintains 62% effective hydration when combined with starter water

ingredients.name: Sourdough Starter (100% Hydration)
ingredients.sourcedFrom: 5/5 pure SD recipes; Perfect Loaf uses 15% of flour
ingredients.rationale: 100g at 100% hydration contributes 50g flour + 50g water. ~22% of total flour

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.sourcedFrom: Carried from base recipe; 5/5 SD recipes use ~2%

ingredients.name: Diastatic Malt Powder
ingredients.sourcedFrom: PizzaBlab, King Arthur, food science agent
ingredients.rationale: Amylase enzymes produce reducing sugars during bake, compensating for sourdough's pH-inhibited Maillard reaction at 550°F
ingredients.note: Substitute: 5g granulated sugar (1% of total flour) if malt is unavailable. Add at the same step. At 1%, sugar won't interfere with gluten development during fermentolyse — that only matters at 15%+. Sugar adds reducing sugars directly but lacks the enzymatic activity of diastatic malt.

ingredients.name: Low-Moisture Mozzarella
ingredients.note: Low-moisture, high-fat, whole milk mozzarella — shreds clean and melts right

ingredients.name: Parmigiano-Reggiano or Pecorino Romano
ingredients.note: Freshly grated — adds a savory base layer under the mozzarella

states.title: Prepare Workspace
states.direction: Gather all vessels, equipment, and ingredients. Weigh out bread flour, water, starter, salt, and diastatic malt powder into separate containers. Ensure your sourdough starter is ripe and active.
states.exit_condition: All ingredients weighed, vessels and equipment laid out, starter is ripe and active

notes.text: The starter must be at peak activity — doubled in size, domed, and bubbly throughout. Test with a small pinch in water (it should float) before weighing out your 100g. If it's not ready, feed it 4-8 hours before mixing.

states.title: Mix Fermentolyse
states.direction: In the large mixing bowl (V1), combine 413g bread flour, 238g water, and 100g sourdough starter. Add 4g diastatic malt powder — or if substituting, add 5g granulated sugar instead. Mix with a wet hand or dough whisk until no dry flour remains. Do not add salt yet.
states.exit_condition: All ingredients combined into a shaggy mass with no dry flour visible. Salt is withheld.

notes.text: This is a fermentolyse, not a true autolyse — the starter's enzymes are active during the rest, beginning fermentation and gluten development simultaneously.

states.title: Fermentolyse Rest
states.direction: Cover the bowl (V1) with plastic wrap and let the dough rest for 30 minutes at room temperature. The starter begins fermenting while the flour hydrates.
states.exit_condition: 30 minutes elapsed, dough is more cohesive and slightly extensible

states.title: Add Salt & Hand Mix
states.direction: Sprinkle 8g salt over the dough. Wet your hands and mix the salt in by squeezing the dough through your fingers and folding it over itself repeatedly for 2-3 minutes until the salt is fully incorporated and no gritty texture remains.
states.exit_condition: Salt fully dissolved into dough, no gritty texture. Dough is slightly tighter than before salt addition.

notes.text: Salt strengthens gluten and controls fermentation rate. Adding it after the fermentolyse rest allows the flour to hydrate without interference.

states.title: Stretch & Fold Sets
states.direction: Perform 3 sets of stretch-and-fold at 30-minute intervals. For each set: wet your hands, reach under one side of the dough, pull it up and fold over the top. Rotate the bowl 90° and repeat 3 more times (4 folds per set). Cover between sets and let rest 30 minutes before the next set.
states.exit_condition: 3 stretch-and-fold sets complete over ~90 minutes. Dough is noticeably smoother, more elastic, and holds its shape when folded.

notes.text: The dough will feel progressively stronger with each set. By set 3, it should feel smooth and billowy.
If the dough feels very tight after set 2, skip set 3 — over-developing gluten in sourdough can lead to excessive snap-back during shaping.

reminders.prompt: How does the dough feel after each fold set?

states.title: Bulk Rest
states.direction: After the final stretch-and-fold, cover the bowl and let the dough rest undisturbed at room temperature (75–77°F / 24–25°C) until it shows a 25–50% volume increase with visible bubbles at the periphery. Typically 1–2 hours after the last fold.
states.exit_condition: Dough has increased 25–50% in volume with visible bubbles along the edges. Surface appears slightly domed and puffy.

notes.text: Do not wait for a full double — sourdough pizza dough should be slightly underproofed at this stage since cold fermentation continues developing it.

states.title: Round Dough
states.direction: Turn the dough out onto a clean surface. Using both hands, cup the dough and pull it toward you repeatedly to build surface tension. Tuck the edges underneath to form a taut ball. Place back into a lightly oiled bowl (V1), cover with plastic wrap.
states.exit_condition: Dough shaped into a smooth, taut ball with good surface tension, placed in oiled bowl and covered

states.title: Cold Bulk Ferment
states.direction: Transfer the covered bowl (V1) to the refrigerator. Cold ferment for 8–16 hours (overnight). The dough will rise slowly and develop complex flavor.
states.exit_condition: Dough has risen noticeably after 8–16 hours in the fridge

notes.text: Cold fermentation develops complex, tangy flavors. The sourdough LAB remain active at fridge temps, producing lactic and acetic acids.

states.title: Divide Portions
states.direction: Remove the fermented dough from the fridge. Turn it out onto a lightly floured surface. Using a bench scraper, divide into 2 equal portions of approximately 380g each.
states.exit_condition: Dough divided into 2 portions of approximately 380g each

notes.text: The Perfect Loaf recommends 290g dough balls for 30cm personal pizzas. At 380g, you'll get larger NY-style pizzas. Adjust ball size after your first bake.

states.title: Round Portions
states.direction: For each portion, pick up the dough and tuck the edges underneath while rotating to form a very tight ball with a completely closed bottom. Drag the ball along the bench to seal the seam. Place each ball on a parchment-lined sheet tray (V2) sprayed with non-stick spray. Spray the tops with non-stick spray, then cover loosely with plastic wrap. Return to the refrigerator.
states.exit_condition: All portions rounded into tight balls with closed bottoms, on parchment-lined tray, sprayed, covered, and returned to fridge

notes.text: Tight shaping is critical for sourdough pizza — the acid-tightened gluten needs strong surface tension to hold its shape during the cold proof.

states.title: Cold Proof
states.direction: Let the dough balls proof in the refrigerator for 1 to 2 days. Maximum 48 hours — sourdough continues acidifying in the fridge, and beyond 48h risks overacidification and gluten degradation.
states.exit_condition: Dough balls have visibly expanded after 1–2 days in the fridge, surface is smooth and slightly puffy

notes.text: Unlike yeasted dough (which can cold proof up to 72h), sourdough's LAB remain active at fridge temps. Beyond 48h, ongoing acidification degrades gluten structure and depletes browning sugars.
Begin preheating the oven and baking steel at least 45 minutes before you plan to bake.

states.title: Temper Dough
states.direction: Remove the dough balls from the refrigerator and let them sit at room temperature for approximately 6 hours. Sourdough's acid-tightened gluten needs significantly more time to relax than yeasted dough.
states.exit_condition: Dough balls are at room temperature, relaxed, and easy to press with a finger. When poked, the indentation fills back slowly.

notes.text: If the dough still resists stretching after 6 hours, let it rest 5-10 more minutes between stretch attempts — don't force cold sourdough dough.
Start preheating the oven during this step — by the time the dough is tempered, the steel will be fully saturated with heat.

states.title: Preheat Baking Steel
states.direction: Place the baking steel (V3) on the middle oven rack. Preheat the oven to 550°F (288°C). Allow at least 45 minutes for the steel to fully saturate with heat.
states.exit_condition: Oven at 550°F (288°C) and steel fully preheated for at least 45 minutes

notes.text: A fully preheated steel is essential — it provides the intense bottom heat that creates a properly charred crust.

states.title: Stretch Dough
states.direction: Sprinkle the wooden pizza peel (V4) with 7g cornmeal. Place one dough ball on a lightly floured surface. Using your fingertips, press from the center outward, pushing air toward the edges to form the crust rim. Pick up the dough and drape it over your knuckles, gently stretching and rotating until you have a 30–33cm (12–13 inch) disc. Transfer to the cornmeal-dusted peel.
states.exit_condition: Dough stretched to a 30–33cm disc with puffy edge crust, resting on cornmeal-dusted peel

notes.text: Sourdough pizza dough may feel tighter than yeasted dough — if it resists stretching, let it rest 5 minutes on the counter and try again.
Never roll pizza dough — rolling pops the gas bubbles that create the airy, puffy crust.
Give the peel a shake before topping to make sure the dough slides freely on the cornmeal.

states.title: Top Pizza
states.direction: Spread 88g raw San Marzano tomato sauce over the dough, leaving a 2cm border for the crust. Grate 20g Parmigiano-Reggiano or Pecorino Romano evenly over the sauce. Top with 175g low-moisture mozzarella, torn or shredded. Place 88g pepperoni on top of the cheese.
states.exit_condition: Pizza topped in order: sauce, grated hard cheese, mozzarella, pepperoni on top

notes.text: Pepperoni goes on top of the cheese so it browns, crisps, and cups up during baking.
Do not overload with sauce or the center will be soggy and the pizza will not slide off the peel.

states.title: Bake Pizza
states.direction: Slide the pizza from the peel onto the preheated steel (V3) with a quick forward-and-back motion. Bake at 550°F (288°C) for 4–5 minutes until the bottom is set and beginning to char. Transfer the pizza (not the steel) to the broiler drawer for 30–60 seconds to finish the top. Repeat for the second pizza.
states.exit_condition: Cheese is bubbly and lightly browned, crust is puffed and golden with charred spots. Bottom has leopard-spotted char from the steel.

notes.text: The broiler finish is especially important for sourdough pizza — the acid-inhibited Maillard reaction means the crust may be paler than yeasted pizza without the broiler's intense radiant heat.
Rotate the pizza halfway through the steel bake if your oven has hot spots.

states.title: Cool & Slice
states.direction: Use the peel to slide the baked pizza onto a wire rack or cutting board. Let it rest for 2–3 minutes. Cut into 8 slices. Serve immediately.
states.exit_condition: Pizza rested, cut into 8 slices, ready to serve

notes.text: A brief rest lets the cheese set slightly so it does not slide off when you pick up a slice.

techniques.name: Fermentolyse (flour + water + starter rest)
techniques.sourcedFrom: Perfect Loaf, Vincenzo's Plate, user preference
techniques.rationale: Allows flour hydration and begins fermentation simultaneously. Simpler than true autolyse for pizza.

techniques.name: Stretch-and-fold over stand mixer
techniques.rationale: Sourdough protease enzymes degrade gluten over time — gentler handling prevents over-development.

techniques.name: Diastatic malt for browning compensation
techniques.sourcedFrom: PizzaBlab, King Arthur, food science research
techniques.rationale: Sourdough pH (3.5-4.5) inhibits Maillard reaction. Malt amylase produces reducing sugars during the bake.

techniques.name: 48h cold ferment ceiling
techniques.sourcedFrom: Virtue Pizza, PizzaMaking.com, food science agent
techniques.rationale: Sourdough LAB remain active at fridge temps. Beyond 48h: acidification degrades gluten and depletes browning sugars.

techniques.name: 6-hour temper time
techniques.rationale: Acetic acid from cold ferment tightens gluten bonds. Cold stiffens proteins. Both compound — SD dough needs more relaxation.

techniques.name: Omit olive oil
techniques.rationale: Strong consensus against oil in pure sourdough pizza dough.

research.strategy: Multi-agent parallel research with 7 agents (6 initial + 1 follow-up). Strategies: pure sourdough recipes, hybrid recipes, food science, home oven constraints, Reddit community, Perfect Loaf deep dive, broiler drawer research.

methods.detail: Heat a dry pan over medium-high heat. Add 1–3 slices of cold pizza and heat for about 2 minutes until the bottom starts to crisp. Add 1–1.5 tsp water and immediately cover the pan. Steam covered for 30 seconds. Uncover, let remaining water boil off, and continue cooking until the bottom is firm and crispy.
350–400°F (175–200°C) for about 5 minutes. Quick and effective, crisps the bottom well.

Maintains ~22% inoculation rate; fermentation timeline scales proportionally
Scales to maintain ~1.7% salt ratio; crucial for flavor and dough strength
Enzyme activity scales with flour weight; maintains browning compensation
Scales with pizza count; coverage ratio remains consistent
Scales with pizza count; low-moisture variety essential at all scales
Scales with pizza count; maintains umami base layer
Scales with pizza count; distribution coverage remains consistent

process_caveats: Bulk fermentation timeline scales: at 2× dough mass, room-temperature bulk will complete ~30-50% faster due to increased thermal mass. Monitor dough volume closely — do not rely solely on timer; use visual indicators (25–50% rise) as primary guide.

Vessel size must increase with dough volume. At 2×, ensure your bulk fermentation bowl is at least 5-6L capacity (a standard large mixing bowl ~8L is adequate). Insufficient headroom prevents proper stretch-and-fold execution.

Bake sequencing matters: two pizzas cannot bake simultaneously on a single steel. At 2×, plan two separate stretch-and-proofs with staggered loading (pizza 1 while pizza 2 tempers), or use two steels if available. Skipping this causes dough loss or uneven bake results.
sources: The Perfect Loaf - Maurizio Leo on sourdough pizza dough fermentation and scaling (https://www.theperfectloaf.com/sourdough-pizza-dough-and-recipes/)
Food Science research on fermentation rate vs. dough mass (Bread Bakers Guild of America resources)

cook_log.summary: First bake — 3-day process. Used 5g sugar substitute (no malt). Dough was easy to work with throughout. Didn't do full 6-hour temper but dough still stretched well. ~8 min on steel + 1.5 min broiler per pizza. Really good — thin, droopy, flexible, slight tang.
notes: Sat 3/22 5:09pm — kitchen 76°F.
Sat 3/22 5:10pm — fermentolyse mixed with 5g sugar substitute, no diastatic malt available.
Sat 3/22 ~5:42pm — salt added.
Sat 3/22 6:12pm — first stretch-and-fold set. Dough ball looked small — questioning how big the pizzas would be.
Completed all 3 S&F sets — dough was easy to work with.
Into fridge for cold bulk ferment (exact time not logged).
Sun 3/23 ~12pm — pulled from fridge, divided into 2 balls. Nearly perfectly equal by eyeball — satisfying. Weight not recorded, estimated ~300g each. Back in fridge for cold proof.
Mon 3/24 — pulled dough to temper. Didn't realize the 6-hour temper was needed. Dough was still a bit chilly but eventually stretched out easily.
Preheated baking steel at 550°F. ~8 min per pizza on steel + ~1.5 min under broiler, monitored closely so nothing burned.
Toppings: Sclafani sauce, TJ's pecorino on the sauce, TJ's low-moisture whole milk mozz, Boar's Head pepperoni.
Really good. A little sourdough tang. Size was good. Very droopy and flexible — thin crust.

photos.alt: Two finished pepperoni pizzas cooling on the counter — one on a wire rack in the foreground, one on a cutting board behind. Both show golden-brown crusts with melted cheese and pepperoni coverage.
Overhead view of a finished pepperoni pizza cooling on a wire rack. Cheese is melted and browned with scattered pepperoni across the surface; the crust edge is thin and lightly charred.
Underside of a slice held up to show the bottom crust. Leopard-spotted char pattern from baking on steel, with an even golden-brown base and scattered dark blisters.
A slice held from the crust end, drooping significantly under its own weight. The tip bends downward past vertical, demonstrating the thin, flexible character of the crust.
Top-down view of a pepperoni slice held above a cutting board with remaining slices. Pepperoni is lightly crisped and cupped, cheese melted evenly across the surface.
Side profile of a slice showing the thin crust edge-on. The crust is notably thin with a slight cornicione rise at the outer edge and minimal puff through the center.

next_time.text: Do the full 6-hour temper — dough was still chilly this time.
Try a different pecorino — TJ's was just OK.

cook_log.summary: Second bake, doubled to 4 pizzas — first time at this volume. Overall success despite some execution bumps (sauce pizza stuck to peel, dough tear on #3). Flavor felt lacking compared to basic NY dough; may try a shorter proof next time.
notes: 4:25pm CDT (Tue 4/8) — fermentolyse start.
4:33pm — dough temp 79.7°F. Warm day. Doubled recipe for 4 pizzas total.
4:59pm — dough temp 80.8°F before adding salt.
~5:05pm — waited 30 min after salt incorporation. Aliquot at 10% (pulled a bit too much dough). Dough super warm; considered preshaping that night.
~5:53pm — first S&F was late. Dough still pretty stiff, still hot at 79.7°F.
~6:28pm — second S&F, 80.2°F. Aliquot at 15%.
~7:30pm — last S&F, 79.7°F. Aliquot at 30%.
~8:34pm — aliquot ~55% (calling effectively 45% due to extra dough in vessel). Turned out dough.
~8:38pm — total weight ~1509g (scale unreliable). Into Cambro in fridge for cold bulk ferment, aliquot placed alongside. 78.4°F before fridge.
Wed 4/9 ~8:28am — total weight 1524g after adding back aliquot. Target 381g per ball.
~8:33am — divided into 4 balls: 384g, 380g, 387g, 382g.
~9:10am — shaped 4 balls, into fridge for cold proof.
Thu 4/10 ~10am — prepped toppings. Made sauce from Sclafani tomatoes following on-file recipe, added chopped fresh basil. Prepared day before to develop flavor.
Fri 4/11 ~6:30am — pulled dough from fridge. Started baking around 9am (~2.5-hour temper). Did not re-shape on bake day as planned.
Full 1-hour preheat at 550°F. Used infrared thermometer to confirm steel at ~530–550°F before launching.
Pizza #1 (Boar's Head pepperoni) — launched perfectly.

Pizza #2 (sauce only) — stuck to peel, dough launched wrong. Recovered by baking as a focaccia-style square. Really liked the result — lots of sauce was satisfying. Simmered leftover sauce with olive oil after for dipping.
Cleaned steel and let oven return to temp before Pizza #3.
Pizza #3 (cheese with fresh basil — vegan) — small dough tear, used basil leaf trick. Overcooked top in broiler, scorched the basil leaves. Best-looking crust of the four.
Pizza #4 (jalapeño pepperoni) — small hole detected at end of bake. Left some seeds intentionally — cheese absorbs the jalapeño spice and flavor. TJ jalapeños work great for this.
All 4 pizzas baked at 550°F throughout.
Cheese: TJ low-moisture whole milk mozz plus Parmigiano Reggiano chunk from HEB (had been in fridge a while). Old TJ parmesan wasn't a fan of; will bring both for guests as extra toppings.

Flavor felt lacking — possibly tired or not hungry, but also wondering if 3-day (possibly 4-day) proof dulled the flavor. May also be that NY-style ingredients don't pair as well with the sourdough base. Might just prefer the basic recipe.
Starter was kind of weak this bake — may have affected dough strength.

photos.alt: Shaped dough ball resting on the countertop after turnout — smooth, taut surface with the glass mixing bowl visible behind it.
Bulk dough in a metal bowl on an OXO digital scale — bubbly, fermented surface showing good activity before dividing into 4 balls.
Sauce-only pizza (#2) on the baking steel inside the oven — dough puffing up around the edges, mis-launched but recovering mid-bake.
Side view of a pepperoni slice (#1) showing the crumb — open, well-aerated crust tapering to a thin crispy center.
Overhead shot of sliced sauce-and-basil pizza (#2) — mix of square and wedge cuts, charred basil leaves scattered across bright red sauce, no cheese.
Closeup of sauce pizza (#2) slice lifted to show the crumb — open, airy interior despite the failed launch. Charred basil on top.
Side view of cheese-and-basil slice (#3) — open, airy interior with large irregular holes throughout the crust. Best fermentation bubbles of the four.
Top view of cheese-and-basil slice (#3) — browned mozzarella with scorched basil leaf from overcooked broiler. Good crumb visible along the cornicione.
Whole jalapeño pepperoni pizza (#4) cooling on a wire rack — generous pepperoni coverage with scattered jalapeño slices, leopard-spotted charring on the cornicione.
Top view of jalapeño pepperoni slice (#4) — flat pepperoni slices, sliced jalapeño rings, melted cheese with browning.
Side profile of jalapeño pepperoni slice (#4) — thin, crispy base with visible jalapeño rings and even crumb structure. Not much rise, possibly overproofed.

next_time.text: Use 1.5x sauce on sauce pizza to prevent overflow.
Cap broiler at 45 seconds for vegan pizzas (sauce-only and cheese/basil) to avoid scorching.
Try 2-day proof — flavor may be better and timing easier to predict.
Plan bake day in advance — know how many days ahead to start the dough based on the event.
Research pizza transport for events (quarter sheets + parchment in Tupperware, possibly layering).
